intro: At the Alcotts’ piano, hymns and Scottish songs rub shoulders with Beethoven’s Fifth. Ives turns that household music into the broad C major melody at the heart of the Concord Sonata.

relations.label: The parlour melody returns
relations.basis: The paired spans lie in the middle parlour-music episode, whose melodic paragraph recurs. Kyle Gann describes its two turns towards Wagner’s wedding tune at https://charlesives.org/node/6616; this link concerns the longer paragraph, not an individually timed quotation. CENS diagonal mean 0.940, sustained 29 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 40.5 s (cache/form/ives-concord-alcotts.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A hymn in two keys
cues.text: The piano sings a hymn-like melody in B♭ while the bass chords belong to A♭. The tune is almost complete already: it is the melody that keeps appearing, in pieces, throughout the Concord Sonata.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann, “Following the Concord Sonata”, section “The Alcotts”: opening human-faith melody in B♭ with A♭ bass chords. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Beth at the spinet
cues.text: In his 1920 essay, Ives points to a “little old spinet-piano” at Orchard House. His picture mingles the Alcott family with Little Women: Beth plays Scottish airs and tries her hand at Beethoven’s Fifth.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “The Alcotts”, paragraph beginning “Concord village”: the spinet and Beth’s playing. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#alcotts

cues.title: Beethoven raises his voice
cues.text: The short-short-short-long figure of Beethoven’s Fifth pushes through the piano chords. It meets another borrowed tune, Missionary Hymn, whose repeated notes also drop by a third. Ives sets them against one another in different keys.
cues.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”: the relationship between Missionary Hymn and the Beethoven figure, and the dissonant climaxes. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Music for the parlour
cues.text: A song-like piano passage brings the music indoors again. Its turns suggest Scottish folk songs; twice it brushes against the wedding music from Wagner’s Lohengrin. Ives lets the parlour piano enjoy itself.
cues.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”: the middle parlour-music episode, Scottish-song idiom and two references to the wedding march from Lohengrin. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Kirkpatrick at Town Hall
cues.text: On 20 January 1939 John Kirkpatrick gives the complete sonata its public première at New York’s Town Hall. He has already played it from memory at a private concert in Cos Cob. The score has been circulating for eighteen years.
cues.evidence: Gann’s chronology: circulation in January 1921, private complete performance at Cos Cob on 28 November 1938, and public première on 20 January 1939. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: The song starts to strain
cues.text: The Scottish-song turns stretch into a tense chromatic passage. The piano chords crowd around the melody, working towards a much broader statement of the sonata’s recurring tune.
cues.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”: the chromatic transition transforms the Scottish-song idiom before the final C major statement. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: C major, with both hands
cues.text: The whole melody opens out in broad C major chords. Its climbing do–re–mi and Beethoven’s repeated-note figure now belong to one continuous tune. The piano seems almost too small for it.
cues.evidence: Gann’s Example 1 and “The Alcotts” identify the complete human-faith melody, its opening scale and Beethoven component, and its final C major setting. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One last B♭
cues.text: As the tune fades, Ives slips back into B♭ for a moment. Then the piano closes on C major, simply and quietly.
cues.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”, final paragraph: B♭ briefly recalled before the last C major chord. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The piano returns to the parlour
transitions.to: B · Scottish songs at the piano
transitions.how: After the Beethoven climax, the recurring melody returns quietly over dissonant piano chords. The next episode separates a song-like upper line from its accompaniment. Scottish turns and a glimpse of Wagner’s wedding music replace the pounding repeated notes.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”: quiet restatement following the climax, then the parlour episode. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: The parlour tune loses its bearings
transitions.from: B · Scottish songs at the piano
transitions.to: Link · The parlour tune grows restless
transitions.how: The piano keeps the parlour tune’s Scottish turns but alters them with chromatic notes. Increasingly crowded chords unsettle the easy accompaniment. The little song grows into a tense link before the broad C major melody.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”: the harmonically ambiguous transition gradually transforms the Scottish-song idiom. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: The hands agree on C major
transitions.from: Link · The parlour tune grows restless
transitions.to: A″ · The whole tune in C major
transitions.how: The chromatic piano passage opens into the complete recurring melody in C major. Both hands play broad chords beneath its do–re–mi opening and Beethoven-derived repeated notes. The fragments that crowded the earlier movements now fit into a single singing phrase.
transitions.evidence: Gann, Example 1 and “The Alcotts”: the complete C major statement and its component phrases. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: B♭ before the last C
transitions.from: A″ · The whole tune in C major
transitions.to: Coda · B♭ remembered, then C major
transitions.how: The broad C major chords grow quieter. Ives briefly brings back B♭, recalling the opening key, then closes with a C major chord. The last change of harmony happens inside the slowing piano phrase.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “The Alcotts”, final paragraph: the dying-away theme, momentary B♭ and final C major chord. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

composer.epithet: He sold life insurance in New York and wrote music in which a hymn across the river could outlast a whole marching band.
facts: His father George Ives; Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; insurance executive at Ives & Myrick
Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata, 1920; 114 Songs, 1922
Danbury bands and hymn singing; the New England of Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
George Ives played his cornet across a pond so that his son could hear what distance did to the sound. He made the boy sing in one key while he accompanied in another, built instruments that could play quarter-tones and tried out the collision of two marching bands. A former Union Army bandmaster, he earned his living teaching and directing music in Danbury, Connecticut. Charles, born there in 1874, grew up with a father for whom a wrong note could be the beginning of an experiment.

The lessons also involved work. By fourteen Charles was a salaried church organist; at seventeen he wrote the Variations on America, putting the tune of God Save the King through a teenager’s display of keyboard tricks. At Yale, which he entered in 1894, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and how to sustain a symphony. His First Symphony was the result: a young American speaking fluent European. George died of a stroke during Charles’s first term. His son kept talking about him for the next sixty years.
